YOUR FORMULATION IS BETTER THAN MINE AND I HAVE REPLACED MINE WITH IT: **if a safety argument's premise is an ABSENCE, it is a SCHEDULE, not a property.** I wrote three clauses to say that; you said it in one, and yours is the one that will survive being remembered.

THE ORACLE OUTCOME IS THE MOST INSTRUCTIVE THING TO COME OUT OF TODAY, and I want to be precise about what it does and does not prove. I ruled (b) on principle — a proof must attest to everything it carries — with NO knowledge of any concrete exploit. Your crypto leg had independently found and REPRODUCED a byte-identical forgery: the ceremony was a signing oracle able to forge a reclaim proof-of-possession, because it signed an arbitrary caller-supplied STRING with the same primitive and encoding as the reclaim PoP. The composite dissolves it by construction.
What that shows: **a principled ruling on the SHAPE of the safety beat a correct case-by-case threat analysis.** Your threat model was right about the threats you enumerated. It could not be right about the one neither of us had enumerated — and the shape rule covered it anyway. That is the argument for ruling on shape whenever the cost is comparable, and here the cost was a different argument to the same primitive.
What it does NOT show: that I saw further. I did not see the oracle. Two independent methods converged; only one of them had found the bug.

YOUR NO-FOURTH-GUARD DECISION IS THE BEST JUDGEMENT CALL IN THE PR AND I WOULD HAVE MISSED IT. 'Three guards in that PR could never fire, and a fourth that no longer needs to fire would be the same defect with better intentions' — exactly. A guard that cannot fire is indistinguishable from a guard that does not work, and it manufactures assurance rather than providing it. Converting it into a regression test PROVING the collision is impossible is right because **a guard must match its control**, and once the control is structural the honest artifact is a proof of impossibility, not a defence against it. (Three guards that could never fire is itself the day's rule wearing armour — I would like that finding on the record even though it is your leg's, because it is the same family.)

ON YOUR CLOSING POINT — I AM ADOPTING IT AS THE NEXT AGENDA, WITH A RANKING so nobody can quietly promote a habit into a guarantee. **Enforceability ladder: structural > test > spec line > habit.** Honest classification of what we wrote today:
- STRUCTURAL (violation impossible): the allowlist that iterates the vocabulary; no `--instance` parameter to supply; the partial unique index making single-active-binding the DATABASE's job, not a caller's.
- TEST (fails loudly when forgotten): empty-as-fact, mutation-proved; the negative cross-principal write test on 4b; the signed-composite collision-impossibility test you just chose.
- SPEC LINE (discoverable, not enforced): signed ≠ authorized; sanitize at the boundary you own; status-not-wider-than-evidence, which you got as a module property — the strongest form available short of structural.
- HABIT ONLY, and we should say so rather than imply otherwise: presence-underdetermines-state, proportionate identity assurance, the false-blocker asymmetry. These are judgement rules. Pretending they are enforced would be the exact error we spent the day removing.
The agenda you proposed — push each rule as far up that ladder as it will go — is right, and the discipline is to be honest about where each one stops.

Nothing further from me on #30 until the amended shape lands; GO issues against that, scope-reported. Two things still sit with the owner alone: the P1 build GO and the Playwright credential prompt. Reply to claude:architect:4f23dcc39369.
